$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}W_{i,j}^{(l)}\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle=\mathbb{E}\frac{\partial}{\partial W_{i,j}^{(l)}}\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}t}{n}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)2}x_{j}^{(l)2}\right\rangle-\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle^{2}\right]. $$

Let $(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$ and $(\bar{\mathbf{x}},\bar{\mathbf{y}})$ be two independent configurations drawn from the Gibbs distribution. The first term is trivial since $x_{i}^{(l)2}=1$ . The second term above can be re-expressed as

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\bar{x}_{i}^{(l)}\bar{x}_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle\right], $$

where the last equality follows by Nishimori identity. Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}W_{i,j}^{(l)}\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle= \displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}t}{n}}\left[1-\mathbb{E}\left\langle X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle\right]. $$

Similar computations yield

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}W_{i}^{(l)\prime}\left\langle y_{i}^{(l)}\right\rangle= \displaystyle\sqrt{\lambda^{(l)}q_{l}(1-t)}\left[1-\mathbb{E}\left\langle X_{i}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}\right\rangle\right]. $$

Plugging back into (3.5), we can provide a lower bound

$$ \displaystyle\psi^{\prime}(t)= \displaystyle\frac{1}{2n}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{i<j}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}-\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda^{(l)}q_{l}X_{i}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}\right\rangle\right]+\sum_{l=1}^{L}\lambda^{(l)}\left(\frac{n-1}{4n}-\frac{q_{l}}{2}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{4}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda^{(l)}\left\langle\left(\mathbf{x}^{(l)}.\mathbf{X}^{(l)}\right)^{2}-2q_{l}\mathbf{x}^{(l)}.\mathbf{X}^{(l)}\right\rangle\right]+\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}(1-2q_{l})}{4}+o(1) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{4}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda^{(l)}\left\langle\left(\mathbf{x}^{(l)}.\mathbf{X}^{(l)}-q_{l}\right)^{2}\right\rangle\right]+\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}(1-2q_{l}-q_{l}^{2})}{4}+o(1) \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}(1-2q_{l}-q_{l}^{2})}{4}+o(1). $$

where we define $\mathbf{x}^{(l)}.\mathbf{X}^{(l)}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{(l)}X_{i}^{(l)}$ as the empirical overlap. Because $t=0$ corresponds to repeating channel (1.7) independently for $n$ times,

$$ \psi(0)=\mathbb{E}\log\left[\sum_{(x,y)\in\{\pm 1\}^{L+L_{1}}}p(x,y|Z)\exp\left(\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sqrt{\lambda^{(l)}q_{l}}A^{(l)\prime}x^{(l)}\right)\right]. $$

Since $F_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=\psi(0)+\int_{0}^{1}\psi^{\prime}(t)\mathrm{d}t$ and $\psi^{\prime}(t)$ is lower bounded in (3.6), we find

$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}F_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\geq\frac{\sum_{l=1}^{L}\lambda^{(l)}}{4}+\sup_{\mathbf{q}\geq 0}\left[\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{\lambda},\mathbf{q})-\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}(q_{l}^{2}+2q_{l})}{4}\right]. $$

### 3.2 Overlap Concentration via Perturbation by BEC

For the converse upper bound, it will be useful to establish concentration of the overlap in this inference problem. To this end, inspired by the techniques introduced in Montanari (2008); Lelarge and Miolane (2019), we add a small perturbation to the model via a binary erasure channel. This will force correlation decay among the different coordinates in a sample. To set the stage of the small perturbation, we introduce a factor graph $(V,F,Z,E)$ of our observation model, which is defined to be a bipartite graph. To be precise, $|V|=n$ are vertices corresponding to variable nodes, $V_{i}=(X_{i},Y_{i})$ for each $i\in[n]$ ; $|F|=n(n-1)/2$ corresponds to function nodes standing for memoryless observations, $F_{a}=(A_{i,j}^{(1)},\ldots,A_{i,j}^{(L)})$ for each pair $a=(i,j)$ with $1\leq i<j\leq n$ . Edge set $E$ characterizes how each $F_{a}$ depends on $V$ , namely $F_{(i,j)}$ only connects to $V_{i}$ and $V_{j}$ . Moreover, we also add nodes $Z_{i}$ corresponding to additionally observed side information. Each $Z_{i}$ connects to $V_{i}$ only. See Figure 9 for an illustration of this factor graph, where circles indicate observed variables and squares indicate variables to be recovered.

*Figure 9: Factor graph of the observation model when $n=4$ .*

Remark: Compared to the sparse graph in Montanari (2008), our bipartite graph has asignificantly larger number of function nodes ( $n(n-1)/2$ compared to the number $n$ of variable nodes). However, each function node’s signal strength $\frac{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}{n}$ decays with respect to $n$ , thus facilitating applications of lemmas from Montanari (2008).

We are now ready to formally define the perturbation in the form of erasure channels. Suppose we additionally observe,

$$ V_{i}(\epsilon)=\mathsf{BEC}_{\epsilon}(V_{i})=\left\{\begin{aligned} &V_{i}&\text{with probability }\epsilon,\\
&\ast&\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right. $$

Upon observing this additional information, we first justify that the perturbed free energy does not deviate too much from the original free energy. For any configuration $\mathbf{v}=(v_{1},\ldots,v_{n})\in\{\pm 1\}^{n\times(L+L_{1})}$ , define $\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}=(\widetilde{v}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{v}_{n})$ by

$$ \widetilde{v}_{i}=v_{i}\mathbbm{1}\{V_{i}(\epsilon)=\ast\}+V_{i}\mathbbm{1}\{V_{i}(\epsilon)\neq\ast\}. $$

This notion allows a very convenient expression for the normalizing constant $Z_{n,\epsilon}$ of $p(\cdot|\mathbf{V}(\epsilon),\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle Z_{n,\epsilon}:= \displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{v}}p(\mathbf{v}|\mathbf{V}(\epsilon),\mathbf{Z})e^{H_{n}(\mathbf{v})}=\sum_{\mathbf{v}}\left(\prod_{i:V_{i}(\epsilon)\neq\ast}\mathbbm{1}\{v_{i}=V_{i}\}\right)\left(\prod_{i:V_{i}(\epsilon)=\ast}p(v_{i}|Z_{i})\right)e^{H_{n}(\mathbf{v})}. $$

Denote $\mathcal{I}=\{i\in[n]:V_{i}(\epsilon)=\ast\}$ , then we find

$$ \displaystyle Z_{n,\epsilon}= \displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{v}_{\mathcal{I}}}\left(\prod_{i\in\mathcal{I}}p(v_{i}|Z_{i})\right)e^{H_{n}(\mathbf{v}_{\mathcal{I}}\oplus\mathbf{V}_{\mathcal{I}^{c}})} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{v}_{\mathcal{I}}}\left(\sum_{\mathbf{v}_{\mathcal{I}^{c}}}\prod_{i\notin\mathcal{I}}p(v_{i}|Z_{i})\right)\left(\prod_{i\in\mathcal{I}}p(v_{i}|Z_{i})\right)e^{H_{n}(\mathbf{v}_{\mathcal{I}},\mathbf{V}_{\mathcal{I}^{c}})} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{v}}\prod_{i}p(v_{i}|Z_{i})e^{H_{n}(\widetilde{\mathbf{v}})}. $$

#### Proposition 3.1.

Define pertubed normalized free energy as $F_{n,\epsilon}=\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\log Z_{n,\epsilon}$ . This quantity is Lipschitz in $\epsilon$ , i.e. there exists $C>0$ (independent of $n$ ) such that for any $\epsilon,\epsilon^{\prime}\in[0,1]$ , we have

$$ |F_{n,\epsilon}-F_{n,\epsilon^{\prime}}|\leq C|\epsilon-\epsilon^{\prime}|. $$

#### Proof.

To establish this result, we consider a more general setting in which revelation probabilities for each $V_{i}$ can be different: $\mathbb{P}(V_{i}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})=V_{i})=\epsilon_{i}$ . We can still define $F_{n,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}$ and $Z_{n,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}$ . Using the law of total probability,

$$ \displaystyle F_{n,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}= \displaystyle\frac{\epsilon_{1}}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\log\left(\sum_{\mathbf{v}}p(\mathbf{v}|\mathbf{Z})e^{H_{n}(\widetilde{\mathbf{v}})}\right)\bigg|V_{1}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\neq\ast\right]+\frac{1-\epsilon_{1}}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\log\left(\sum_{\mathbf{v}}p(\mathbf{v}|\mathbf{Z})e^{H_{n}(\widetilde{\mathbf{v}})}\right)\bigg|V_{1}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})=\ast\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\epsilon_{1}}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\log\left(\sum_{\mathbf{v}}p(\mathbf{v}|\mathbf{Z})e^{H_{n}(V_{1},\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}_{-1})}\right)\right]+\frac{1-\epsilon_{1}}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\log\left(\sum_{\mathbf{v}}p(\mathbf{v}|\mathbf{Z})e^{H_{n}(v_{1},\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}_{-1})}\right)\right]. $$

Consequently,

$$ \frac{\partial F_{n,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}}{\partial\epsilon_{1}}=\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\log\left(\sum_{\mathbf{v}}p(\mathbf{v}|\mathbf{Z})e^{H_{n}(V_{1},\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}_{-1})}\right)\right]-\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\log\left(\sum_{\mathbf{v}}p(\mathbf{v}|\mathbf{Z})e^{H_{n}(v_{1},\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}_{-1})}\right)\right]. $$

Define a Hamiltonian $H^{\prime}_{n}(\mathbf{v})=\sum_{2\leq i<j}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}A^{(l)}_{i,j}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}$ and let $\langle\cdot\rangle$ denote the expectation with respect to the Gibbs measure corresponding to $H_{n}^{\prime}$ . Then we can write

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial F_{n,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}}{\partial\epsilon_{1}}= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\log\left\langle\exp\left(\sum_{j\geq 2}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}A^{(l)}_{1,j}X_{1}^{(l)}\widetilde{x}_{j}^{(l)}\right)\right\rangle\right] \displaystyle-\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\log\left\langle\sum_{v_{1}}p(v_{1}|Z_{1})\exp\left(\sum_{j\geq 2}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}A^{(l)}_{1,j}x_{1}^{(l)}\widetilde{x}_{j}^{(l)}\right)\right\rangle\right]=:T_{1}-T_{2}. $$

Let $\mathbb{E}_{1}$ represent taking expectation over $(W_{1,j})_{j\geq 2}$ only. Since $(W_{1,j})_{j\geq 2}$ is independent of $H^{\prime}_{n}$ defined above, $\mathbb{E}_{1}$ can be alternated with $\langle\cdot\rangle$ . In addition, applying Jenson’s inequality on $\log(\cdot)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle T_{1}\leq \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\log\left\langle\mathbb{E}_{1}\exp\left(\sum_{j\geq 2}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}X_{1}^{(l)2}X_{j}^{(l)}\widetilde{x}_{j}^{(l)}+\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}W^{(l)}_{1,j}X_{1}^{(l)}\widetilde{x}_{j}^{(l)}\right)\right\rangle\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\log\left\langle\exp\left(\sum_{j\geq 2}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}X_{j}^{(l)}\widetilde{x}_{j}^{(l)}+\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{2n}\right)\right\rangle\right]\leq\frac{3\sum_{l}\lambda^{(l)}}{2n}. $$

On the other hand, applying Jenson’s inequality to the $\exp(\cdot)$ function, we have

$$ \displaystyle T_{1}\geq \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j\geq 2}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}X_{1}^{(l)2}X_{j}^{(l)}\left\langle\widetilde{x}_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle+\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}W^{(l)}_{1,j}X_{1}^{(l)}\left\langle\widetilde{x}_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j\geq 2}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}X_{j}^{(l)}\left\langle\widetilde{x}_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle\right]\geq\frac{\sum_{l}\lambda^{(l)}}{n}. $$

In the same way, we can also show $|T_{2}|$ is of order $O(1/n)$ . As a result, we would have $\left|\frac{\partial F_{n,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}}{\partial\epsilon_{1}}\right|\leq\frac{C}{n}$ . We set $\epsilon_{1}=\cdots=\epsilon_{n}$ to conclude that $\left|\frac{\partial F_{n,\epsilon}}{\partial\epsilon}\right|\leq C$ , thus finishing the proof. ∎

This perturbation ensures decorrelation in the posterior distribution, as established in (Montanari, 2008, Lemma 3.1). We recall the result for the sake of completeness.

#### Lemma 3.1 (Montanari (2008)).

Let $\epsilon\sim U[0,n^{-1/2}]$ independent of everything else, the expected conditional mutual information between $V_{i}$ and $V_{j}$ decays in n. Formally, we have,

$$ \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}\left[\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i,j}I(V_{i};V_{j}|\mathbf{V}(\epsilon),\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A})\right]\leq\frac{C}{n}. $$

We use this correlation decay to establish overlap concentration for the perturbed posterior. To this end, we follow the strategy introduced in (Lelarge and Miolane, 2019, Proposition 24).

#### Lemma 3.2.

Let $\mathbf{v}=(v_{1},\ldots,v_{n})$ and $\bar{\mathbf{v}}=(\bar{v}_{1},\ldots,\bar{v}_{n})$ denote two independent configurations sampled from the posterior conditioned on $(\mathbf{V}(\epsilon),\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A})$ , with each $v_{i}=\left(x_{i},y_{i}\right)$ and $\bar{v}_{i}=\left(\bar{x}_{i},\bar{y}_{i}\right)$ . Denote the empirical overlap and its expectation (under the posterior) respectively as

$$ \mathbf{v}.\bar{\mathbf{v}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}\bar{v}_{i}^{\top},\quad Q=\left\langle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}\bar{v}_{i}^{\top}\right\rangle. $$

Under the above mentioned perturbation,

$$ \mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle\left\|\mathbf{v}.\bar{\mathbf{v}}-Q\right\|^{2}\right\rangle\right]\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}0. $$

#### Proof.

First, we expand the squared residual,

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle\left\|\mathbf{v}.\bar{\mathbf{v}}-Q\right\|^{2}\right\rangle=\left\langle\left\|\mathbf{v}.\bar{\mathbf{v}}\right\|^{2}\right\rangle-\left\|\left\langle\mathbf{v}.\bar{\mathbf{v}}\right\rangle\right\|^{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\left\langle\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i,j}\mathrm{Tr}\left(v_{i}\bar{v}_{i}^{\top}v_{j}\bar{v}_{j}^{\top}\right)\right\rangle-\mathrm{Tr}\left(\left\langle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}v_{i}\bar{v}_{i}^{\top}\right\rangle\left\langle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j}v_{j}\bar{v}_{j}^{\top}\right\rangle\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i,j}\mathrm{Tr}\left[\left\langle v_{i}v_{j}^{\top}\right\rangle^{2}-\left(\left\langle v_{i}\right\rangle\left\langle v_{j}\right\rangle^{\top}\right)^{2}\right]. $$

Since every $v_{i}$ is bounded and $\mathrm{Tr}(A^{2}-B^{2})=\mathrm{Tr}((A-B)(A+B))$ for square matrices,

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle\left\|\mathbf{v}.\bar{\mathbf{v}}-Q\right\|^{2}\right\rangle \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\frac{C}{n^{2}}\sum_{i,j}\left\|\left\langle v_{i}v_{j}^{\top}\right\rangle-\left\langle v_{i}\right\rangle\left\langle v_{j}\right\rangle^{\top}\right\| \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{C}{n^{2}}\sum_{i,j}\left\|\sum_{v_{i},v_{j}}v_{i}v_{j}^{\top}\left[p(V_{i}=v_{i},V_{j}=v_{j}\big|\mathbf{V}(\epsilon),\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A})-p(V_{i}=v_{i}\big|\mathbf{V}(\epsilon),\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A})p(V_{j}=v_{j}\big|\mathbf{V}(\epsilon),\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A})\right]\right\| \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\frac{C}{n^{2}}\sum_{i,j}\sum_{v_{i},v_{j}}\left|p(V_{i}=v_{i},V_{j}=v_{j}\big|\mathbf{V}(\epsilon),\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A})-p(V_{i}=v_{i}\big|\mathbf{V}(\epsilon),\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A})p(V_{j}=v_{j}\big|\mathbf{V}(\epsilon),\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A})\right| \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\frac{C}{n^{2}}\sum_{i,j}\text{D}_{\text{TV}}(p(V_{i},V_{j}\big|\mathbf{V}(\epsilon),\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A}),p(V_{i}\big|\mathbf{V}(\epsilon),\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A})\otimes p(V_{j}\big|\mathbf{V}(\epsilon),\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A})). $$

Applying Pinsker’s inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle\left\|\mathbf{v}.\bar{\mathbf{v}}-Q\right\|^{2}\right\rangle \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\frac{C}{n^{2}}\sum_{i,j}\text{D}_{\text{TV}}(p(V_{i},V_{j}\big|\mathbf{V}(\epsilon),\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A}),p(V_{i}\big|\mathbf{V}(\epsilon),\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A})\otimes p(V_{j}\big|\mathbf{V}(\epsilon),\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A})) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\frac{C}{n^{2}}\sum_{i,j}I\left(V_{i};V_{j}|\mathbf{V}(\epsilon),\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A}\right). $$

To finish this lemma, it suffices to take expectation and apply Lemma 3.1. ∎

Finally, using Nishimori identity we have

$$ \mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle\left\|\mathbf{v}.\mathbf{V}-Q\right\|^{2}\right\rangle\right]\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}0. $$

### 3.3 Upper Bound: Aizenman-Sims-Starr scheme

With the convention $F_{0,\epsilon_{0}}=0$ , we have $F_{n,\epsilon_{n}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(k+1)F_{k+1,\epsilon_{k+1}}-kF_{k,\epsilon_{k}}$ . Define

$$ \displaystyle B_{n}= \displaystyle(n+1)F_{n+1,\epsilon_{n+1}}-nF_{n,\epsilon_{n}}=\mathbb{E}\log Z_{n+1,\epsilon_{n+1}}-\mathbb{E}\log Z_{n,\epsilon_{n}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\log\left(\sum_{\mathbf{v},v_{n+1}}p(\mathbf{v}|\mathbf{Z})p(v_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})e^{H_{n+1}(\widetilde{\mathbf{v}},\widetilde{v}_{n+1})}\right)-\mathbb{E}\log\left(\sum_{\mathbf{v}}p(\mathbf{v}|\mathbf{Z})e^{H_{n}(\widetilde{\mathbf{v}})}\right), $$

in which $\mathbf{v}$ is the collection of first $n$ variables. Now we turn to compare

$$ H_{n+1}(\mathbf{x},x_{n+1})=\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{i<j\leq n+1}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n+1}}W_{i,j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}+\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n+1}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)} $$

with $H_{n}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{i<j}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}W_{i,j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}+\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}$ . In order to adjust the change of denominator from $n$ to $n+1$ in the coefficients before $\{W_{i,j}^{(l)},i<j\leq n\}$ , let’s introduce $\widetilde{W}_{i,j}^{(l)}\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ independent of everything else. Noting $\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}}W_{i,j}^{(l)}\overset{d}{=}\sqrt{\frac{1}{n+1}}W_{i,j}^{(l)}+\sqrt{\frac{1}{n(n+1)}}\widetilde{W}_{i,j}^{(l)}$ in the definition of $H_{n}$ , we can decompose $H_{n+1}$ into

$$ H_{n+1}(\mathbf{x},x_{n+1})=H_{n}(\mathbf{x})-\delta(\mathbf{x})+\sum_{l=1}^{L}s_{l}(\mathbf{x})x_{n+1}^{(l)},\quad s_{l}(\mathbf{x}):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n+1}}A_{i,n+1}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}, $$

where $s_{l}(\mathbf{x})$ is used to characterize how $\mathbf{x}$ influences $x_{n+1}$ , while

$$ \delta(\mathbf{x}):=\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n(n+1)}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}+\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n(n+1)}}\widetilde{W}_{i,j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)} $$

is a technical term to adjust changes in denominator from $n$ to $n+1$ . From now on, we use $\langle\cdot\rangle$ to denote the expectation over Gibbs distribution defined by Hamiltonian $H_{n}$ . Therefore, (3.12) becomes,

$$ B_{n}=\mathbb{E}\log\left\langle\sum_{v_{n+1}}p(v_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})e^{-\delta(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}})+\sum_{l}s_{l}(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}})\widetilde{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}}\right\rangle. $$

Now we proceed by incorporating some intuitive mean field approximations, which will be rigorously proved in the next subsection. Expanding their respective definitions,

$$ \displaystyle s_{l}(\mathbf{x})x_{n+1}^{(l)}= \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n+1}x_{i}^{(l)}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{n+1}^{(l)}x_{n+1}^{(l)}+\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n+1}}W_{i,n+1}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{n+1}^{(l)} $$

is found to be approximated by $s_{l}^{0}x_{n+1}^{(l)}+\frac{\lambda^{(l)}-\lambda^{(l)}Q_{l}}{2}$ where

$$ s_{l}^{0}:=\lambda^{(l)}Q_{l}X_{n+1}^{(l)}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}W_{i,n+1}^{(l)}\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)}\right\rangle. $$

Besides,

$$ \displaystyle\delta(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}n}{2(n+1)}\left(\mathbf{x}^{(l)}.\mathbf{X}^{(l)}\right)^{2}-\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{2(n+1)}+\sum_{i<j}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n(n+1)}}\widetilde{W}_{i,j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)} $$

will be approximated by

$$ \delta^{0}:=\sum_{l=1}^{L}\left[\frac{\lambda^{(l)}Q_{l}^{2}+\lambda^{(l)}}{4}+\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}\frac{\sqrt{\lambda^{(l)}}}{n}\widetilde{W}_{i,j}^{(l)}\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle\right]. $$

These intuitions build upon Lemma 3.2, as overlaps $\mathbf{x}^{(l)}.\mathbf{X}^{(l)}$ concentrate near $Q_{l}$ under $\langle\cdot\rangle$ . Proof of the following lemma is postponed to next subsection.

#### Lemma 3.3.

Similar to the notion in (3.12), we write

$$ B_{n}^{0}:=\mathbb{E}\log\sum_{v_{n+1}}p(v_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})e^{-\delta^{0}+\sum_{l}s_{l}^{0}\widetilde{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}+\frac{\lambda^{(l)}-\lambda^{(l)}Q_{l}}{2}}. $$

Then we have $\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}|B_{n}-B_{n}^{0}|\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}0$ .

#### Proof of Proposition 1.1.

Using Proposition 3.1 and Cesaro sum,

$$ \limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}F_{n}\leq\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}F_{n,\epsilon_{n}}\leq\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}B_{n}\leq\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}B_{n}^{0}. $$

While for every $n$ , since $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}W_{i,n+1}^{(l)}\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)}\right\rangle$ equals in law to $\sqrt{\lambda^{(l)}Q_{l}}\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ , it holds

$$ B_{n}^{0}\leq\sup_{\boldsymbol{q}\geq 0}\mathbb{E}\log\left[\sum_{(x,y)\in\{\pm 1\}^{L+L_{1}}}p(x,y|Z)\exp\left(\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sqrt{\lambda^{(l)}q_{l}}A^{(l)\prime}x^{(l)}\right)\right]+\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}(1-2q_{l}-q_{l}^{2})}{4}. $$

Combined with the other bound (3.7) shown in Section 3.1, the proof of Proposition 1.1 is complete. ∎

### 3.4 Proof of Lemma 3.3

Define respectively that

$$ \displaystyle U_{1}= \displaystyle\left\langle\sum_{v_{n+1}}p(v_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})e^{-\delta(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}})+\sum_{l}s_{l}(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}})\widetilde{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}}\right\rangle, \displaystyle\quad U_{2}= \displaystyle\sum_{v_{n+1}}p(v_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})e^{-\delta^{0}+\sum_{l}s_{l}^{0}\widetilde{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}+\frac{\lambda^{(l)}-\lambda^{(l)}Q_{l}}{2}}. $$

As a result, Lemma 3.3 can be restated as $\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}|\mathbb{E}\log U_{1}-\mathbb{E}\log U_{2}|\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}0$ .

#### Lemma 3.4.

It holds that $\lim_{n\rightarrow}\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}\mathbb{E}|U_{1}-U_{2}|^{2}=0$ .

#### Proof.

Write $\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}}$ as taking expectation over $(\widetilde{W}_{i,j}^{(l)})_{1\leq i<j\leq n}$ only, and $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{W}_{n+1}}$ as taking taking expectation over $(W_{i,n+1}^{(l)})_{1\leq i\leq n}$ only. We can exchange $\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}}$ (or $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{W}_{n+1}}$ ) with $\langle\cdot\rangle$ because these standard normals are independent to $\langle\cdot\rangle$ . Plug MGF $\mathbb{E}e^{tW}=e^{t^{2}/2}$ for standard normal $W$ and $Q_{l}=\frac{1}{n}\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)}\right\rangle^{2}$ , we first compute

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}U_{2}^{2}= \displaystyle\sum_{v_{n+1},\bar{v}_{n+1}}p(v_{n+1},\bar{v}_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{\mathbf{W}},\mathbf{W}_{n+1}}e^{-2\delta^{0}+\sum_{l}s_{l}^{0}\left(\widetilde{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}+\widetilde{\bar{x}}_{n+1}^{(l)}\right)+\lambda^{(l)}-\lambda^{(l)}Q_{l}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{v_{n+1},\bar{v}_{n+1}}p(v_{n+1},\bar{v}_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})\prod_{l}\exp\Bigg\{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}-\lambda^{(l)}Q_{l}^{2}}{2}-\sum_{i<j\leq n}\frac{2\lambda^{(l)}}{n^{2}}\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle^{2} \displaystyle\quad+\lambda^{(l)}Q_{l}\left(X_{n+1}^{(l)}\widetilde{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}+X_{n+1}^{(l)}\widetilde{\bar{x}}_{n+1}^{(l)}+\widetilde{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}\widetilde{\bar{x}}_{n+1}^{(l)}\right)\Bigg\}. $$

Moreover, since

$$ \sum_{i<j\leq n}\frac{2\lambda^{(l)}}{n^{2}}\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle^{2}=\lambda^{(l)}\left(\mathbf{x}^{(l)}.\mathbf{X}^{(l)}\right)^{2}+o(1)=\lambda^{(l)}Q_{l}^{2}+o(1), $$

we can further simplify

$$ \mathbb{E}U_{2}^{2}=\sum_{v_{n+1},\bar{v}_{n+1}}p(v_{n+1},\bar{v}_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})e^{\sum_{l}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}-3\lambda^{(l)}Q_{l}^{2}}{2}+\lambda^{(l)}Q_{l}\left(X_{n+1}^{(l)}\widetilde{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}+X_{n+1}^{(l)}\widetilde{\bar{x}}_{n+1}^{(l)}+\widetilde{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}\widetilde{\bar{x}}_{n+1}^{(l)}\right)}+o(1). $$

Now we use MGF again to find,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}}\exp\left[\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n(n+1)}}\widetilde{W}_{i,j}^{(l)}\left(x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}+\bar{x}_{i}^{(l)}\bar{x}_{j}^{(l)}\right)\right]= \displaystyle\exp\left[\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n(n+1)}\left(1+x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\bar{x}_{i}^{(l)}\bar{x}_{j}^{(l)}\right)\right], \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{W}_{n+1}}\exp\left(\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n+1}}W_{i,n+1}^{(l)}\left(x_{i}^{(l)}x_{n+1}^{(l)}+\bar{x}_{i}^{(l)}\bar{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}\right)\right)= \displaystyle\exp\left[\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n+1}\left(1+x_{i}^{(l)}x_{n+1}^{(l)}\bar{x}_{i}^{(l)}\bar{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}\right)\right]. $$

Next, we compute

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}U_{1}^{2}= \displaystyle\left\langle\sum_{v_{n+1},\bar{v}_{n+1}}p(v_{n+1},\bar{v}_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{\mathbf{W}},\mathbf{W}_{n+1}}e^{-\delta(\mathbf{x})-\delta(\bar{\mathbf{x}})+\sum_{l}s_{l}(\mathbf{x})\widetilde{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}+s_{l}(\bar{\mathbf{x}})\widetilde{\bar{x}}_{n+1}^{(l)}}\right\rangle \displaystyle= \displaystyle\Bigg\langle\sum_{v_{n+1},\bar{v}_{n+1}}p(v_{n+1},\bar{v}_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})\prod_{l}\exp\Bigg\{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{2}-\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{2}\left(\mathbf{x}^{(l)}.\mathbf{X}^{(l)}\right)^{2}-\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{2}\left(\bar{\mathbf{x}}^{(l)}.\mathbf{X}^{(l)}\right)^{2} \displaystyle\quad-\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{2}\left(\mathbf{x}^{(l)}.\bar{\mathbf{x}}^{(l)}\right)^{2}+\lambda^{(l)}\left(\mathbf{x}^{(l)}.\mathbf{X}^{(l)}\right)X_{n+1}^{(l)}\widetilde{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}+\lambda^{(l)}\left(\bar{\mathbf{x}}^{(l)}.\mathbf{X}^{(l)}\right)X_{n+1}^{(l)}\widetilde{\bar{x}}_{n+1}^{(l)} \displaystyle\quad+\lambda^{(l)}\left(\mathbf{x}^{(l)}.\bar{\mathbf{x}}^{(l)}\right)x_{n+1}^{(l)}\widetilde{\bar{x}}_{n+1}^{(l)}\Bigg\}\Bigg\rangle+o(1). $$

Define for any triple $(r_{1},r_{2},r_{3})$ where $r_{j}=(r_{j}^{(1)},\ldots,r_{j}^{(L)})$ the following mapping,

$$ \displaystyle f(r_{1},r_{2},r_{3})= \displaystyle\sum_{v_{n+1},\bar{v}_{n+1}}p(v_{n+1},\bar{v}_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})\exp\Bigg(\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{2}+\lambda^{(l)}r_{1}^{(l)}X_{n+1}^{(l)}\widetilde{x}_{n+1}^{(l)} \displaystyle\quad+r_{2}^{(l)}X_{n+1}^{(l)}\widetilde{\bar{x}}_{n+1}^{(l)}+r_{3}^{(l)}x_{n+1}^{(l)}\widetilde{\bar{x}}_{n+1}^{(l)}-\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{2}(r_{1}^{(l)2}+r_{2}^{(l)2}+r_{3}^{(l)2})\Bigg). $$

Equipped with this notion, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}U_{2}^{2}= \displaystyle f(Q,Q,Q)+o(1), \displaystyle\mathbb{E}U_{1}^{2}= \displaystyle\left\langle f(\mathbf{x}.\mathbf{X},\bar{\mathbf{x}}.\mathbf{X},\mathbf{x}.\bar{\mathbf{x}})\right\rangle+o(1). $$

For each $j\in[3]$ and $l\in[L]$ , it holds that $\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial r_{j}^{(l)}}\right|$ is bounded by some positive constant only depending on $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ . Therefore, $f$ is Lipschitz in each of its arguments. We conclude $\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}\left|\mathbb{E}U_{1}^{2}-\mathbb{E}U_{2}^{2}\right|\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}0$ from Lemma 3.2. We can also compute

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}U_{1}U_{2}= \displaystyle\left\langle\sum_{v_{n+1},\bar{v}_{n+1}}p(v_{n+1},\bar{v}_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{\mathbf{W}},\mathbf{W}_{n+1}}e^{-\delta(\mathbf{x})-\delta^{0}+\sum_{l}s_{l}(\mathbf{x})\widetilde{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}+s_{l}^{0}\widetilde{\bar{x}}_{n+1}^{(l)}+\frac{\lambda^{(l)}-\lambda^{(l)}Q_{l}}{2}}\right\rangle \displaystyle= \displaystyle\left\langle f(\mathbf{x}.\mathbf{X},{\mathbf{b}}.\mathbf{X},\mathbf{x}.{\mathbf{b}})\right\rangle+o(1), $$

where $b^{(l)}_{i}=\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)}\right\rangle$ , ${\mathbf{b}}^{(l)}.\mathbf{x}^{(l)}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}b_{i}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}$ and ${\mathbf{b}}^{(l)}.\mathbf{X}^{(l)}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}b_{i}^{(l)}X_{i}^{(l)}$ . Once again, we would conclude $\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}\left|\mathbb{E}U_{1}U_{2}-\mathbb{E}U_{2}^{2}\right|\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}0$ from Lemma 3.2 and Nishimori identity. The desired $L^{2}$ convergence now follows. ∎

#### Lemma 3.5.

There exists a constant $C$ independent of $n$ such that $\mathbb{E}U_{1}^{-2}+\mathbb{E}U_{2}^{-2}\leq C$ .

#### Proof.

Using Jensen inequality,

$$ \displaystyle U_{1}^{-2}\leq \displaystyle\left(\sum_{v_{n+1}}p(v_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})e^{-\left\langle\delta(\mathbf{x})\right\rangle+\sum_{l}\left\langle s_{l}(\mathbf{x})\right\rangle\widetilde{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}}\right)^{-2} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\sum_{v_{n+1}}p(v_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})e^{2\left\langle\delta(\mathbf{x})\right\rangle-2\sum_{l}\left\langle s_{l}(\mathbf{x})\right\rangle\widetilde{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}}. $$

The random variable $\left\langle\delta(\mathbf{x})\right\rangle-\sum_{l}\left\langle s_{l}(\mathbf{x})\right\rangle\widetilde{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}$ has the same law as

$$ \sum_{l}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}Q_{l}^{2}}{2}-\lambda^{(l)}Q_{l}X_{n+1}^{(l)}x_{n+1}^{(l)}+\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}\sum_{l}\lambda^{(l)}Q_{l}}\mathcal{N}(0,1). $$

Thus we have

$$ \mathbb{E}U_{1}^{-2}\leq\mathbb{E}\sum_{v_{n+1}}p(v_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})\mathbb{E}e^{2\left\langle\delta(\mathbf{x})\right\rangle-2\sum_{l}\left\langle s_{l}(\mathbf{x})\right\rangle\widetilde{x}_{n+1}^{(l)}}\leq C. $$

The bound on $\mathbb{E}U_{2}^{-2}$ follows similarly. ∎

Lastly, we use $|\log U_{1}-\log U_{2}|\leq\max(U_{1}^{-1},U_{2}^{-2})|U_{1}-U_{2}|$ and Cauchy Schwarz inequality so that

$$ \mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}|\mathbb{E}\log U_{1}-\mathbb{E}\log U_{2}|\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}\mathbb{E}U_{1}^{-2}+\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}\mathbb{E}U_{2}^{-2}}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}\mathbb{E}|U_{1}-U_{2}|^{2}}\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}0, $$

where the final convergence is evident from Lemmas 3.4 and 3.5. The proof of Lemma 3.3 is now complete.

## 4 Proof of Theorem 1.1, Proposition 1.2 and Proposition 1.3

### 4.1 Asymptotic Normalized MI and MMSE

#### Proof of Theorem 1.1 (i).

By definition,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{A}|\mathbf{Z})= \displaystyle-\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\log\left[\frac{p(\mathbf{A}|\mathbf{Z})}{p(\mathbf{A}|\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z})}\right]=-\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\log\left[\frac{\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}}p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{Z})p(\mathbf{A}|\mathbf{x})}{p(\mathbf{A}|\mathbf{X})}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle-\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\log\left[\frac{\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}}p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{Z})\exp\left(\sum_{l}\sum_{i<j}\sqrt{\lambda^{(l)}/n}A_{i,j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right)}{\exp\left(\sum_{l}\sum_{i<j}\sqrt{\lambda^{(l)}/n}A_{i,j}^{(l)}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}\right)}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{l}\sum_{i<j}\sqrt{\lambda^{(l)}/n}A_{i,j}^{(l)}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}\right]-F_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{l}\frac{(n-1)\lambda^{(l)}}{2n}-F_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda}). $$

Combined with Proposition 1.1, we can establish

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{A}|\mathbf{Z})=\frac{\sum_{l}\lambda^{(l)}}{4}-\sup_{\mathbf{q}\geq 0}\left[\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{\lambda},\mathbf{q})-\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}(q_{l}^{2}+2q_{l})}{4}\right]. $$

Subsequently, since $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z})$ comprise $n$ independent repetitions of the prior $p(x,y,z)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{A},\mathbf{Z}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{Z})+\frac{1}{n}I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{A}|\mathbf{Z})=i_{p}(x,y;z)+\frac{1}{n}I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{A}|\mathbf{Z}) \displaystyle\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}i_{p}(x,y;z)+\frac{\sum_{l}\lambda^{(l)}}{4}-\sup_{\mathbf{q}\geq 0}\left[\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{\lambda},\mathbf{q})-\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}(q_{l}^{2}+2q_{l})}{4}\right], $$

confirming the first assertion (1.12) of this theorem, where $i_{p}(x,y;z)$ is the mutual information between $(x,y)$ and $z$ under prior $p(\cdot)$ . ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 1.1 (ii).

Recall the definition of the free energy from (1.8). By direct differentiation, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda^{(l)}}F_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\frac{\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}}\prod_{i}p(x_{i},y_{i}|Z_{i})\cdot\exp\left(H(\mathbf{x})\right)\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda^{(l)}}H(\mathbf{x})}{\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}}\prod_{i}p(x_{i},y_{i}|Z_{i})\cdot\exp\left(H(\mathbf{x})\right)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\frac{\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}}\prod_{i}p(x_{i},y_{i}|Z_{i})\cdot\exp\left(H(\mathbf{x})\right)\left[\sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{n}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{n\lambda^{(l)}}}W_{i,j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right]}{\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}}\prod_{i}p(x_{i},y_{i}|Z_{i})\cdot\exp\left(H(\mathbf{x})\right)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\frac{\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}}\prod_{i}p(x_{i},y_{i}|Z_{i})\cdot\exp\left(H(\mathbf{x})\right)\left[\sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{2n}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}+\frac{1}{2n}\right]}{\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}}\prod_{i}p(x_{i},y_{i}|Z_{i})\cdot\exp\left(H(\mathbf{x})\right)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{2n^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i<j}\left\langle X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle\right]+\frac{n-1}{4n}, $$

where $\langle\cdot\rangle$ refers to averages under the posterior. Note that we use Gaussian integration by parts in the third step above. Second-order derivatives can be calculated as

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\lambda^{(l_{1})}\partial\lambda^{(l_{2})}}F_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=\frac{1}{2n^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda^{(l_{2})}}\sum_{i<j}\left\langle X_{i}^{(l_{1})}X_{j}^{(l_{1})}x_{i}^{(l_{1})}x_{j}^{(l_{1})}\right\rangle\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{2n^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left\{\sum_{i_{2}<j_{2}}\left[\left\langle\left(\sum_{i<j}X_{i}^{(l_{1})}X_{j}^{(l_{1})}x_{i}^{(l_{1})}x_{j}^{(l_{1})}\right)x^{(l_{2})}_{i_{2}}x^{(l_{2})}_{j_{2}}\right\rangle\right.\right. \displaystyle\qquad\left.\left.-\left\langle\sum_{i<j}X_{i}^{(l_{1})}X_{j}^{(l_{1})}x_{i}^{(l_{1})}x_{j}^{(l_{1})}\right\rangle\left\langle x^{(l_{2})}_{i_{2}}x^{(l_{2})}_{j_{2}}\right\rangle\right]\cdot\left(\frac{1}{n}X^{(l_{2})}_{i_{2}}X^{(l_{2})}_{j_{2}}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{n\lambda^{(l_{2})}}}W_{i_{2},j_{2}}^{(l_{2})}\right)\right\} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{2n^{3}}\mathbb{E}\left\{\sum_{i_{2}<j_{2}}\left[\left\langle\left(\sum_{i<j}X_{i}^{(l_{1})}X_{j}^{(l_{1})}x_{i}^{(l_{1})}x_{j}^{(l_{1})}\right)x^{(l_{2})}_{i_{2}}x^{(l_{2})}_{j_{2}}X^{(l_{2})}_{i_{2}}X^{(l_{2})}_{j_{2}}\right\rangle\right.\right. \displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\left\langle\sum_{i<j}X_{i}^{(l_{1})}X_{j}^{(l_{1})}x_{i}^{(l_{1})}x_{j}^{(l_{1})}\right\rangle\left\langle x^{(l_{2})}_{i_{2}}x^{(l_{2})}_{j_{2}}\right\rangle^{2} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\left.\left.-2\left\langle\sum_{i<j}X_{i}^{(l_{1})}X_{j}^{(l_{1})}x_{i}^{(l_{1})}x_{j}^{(l_{1})}\right\rangle\left\langle x^{(l_{2})}_{i_{2}}x^{(l_{2})}_{j_{2}}X^{(l_{2})}_{i_{2}}X^{(l_{2})}_{j_{2}}\right\rangle\right]\right\} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{2n^{3}}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i_{1}<j_{1}}\sum_{i_{2}<j_{2}}\left(\left\langle x_{i_{1}}^{(l_{1})}x_{j_{1}}^{(l_{1})}x_{i_{2}}^{(l_{2})}x_{j_{2}}^{(l_{2})}\right\rangle-\left\langle x_{i_{1}}^{(l_{1})}x_{j_{1}}^{(l_{1})}\right\rangle\left\langle x_{i_{2}}^{(l_{2})}x_{j_{2}}^{(l_{2})}\right\rangle\right)^{2}\right], $$

where the third display follows from Gaussian integration by parts and the last equation follows from the Nishimori identity. To simplify the notations, we write

$$ \xi_{i,j}^{(l)}=x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}-\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle,\quad i<j,\quad l\in[L], $$

as a centered functional of any replica $\mathbf{x}$ drawn from $\langle\cdot\rangle$ . Moreover, denote

$$ \bar{\xi}_{i,j}^{(l)}=\bar{x}_{i}^{(l)}\bar{x}_{j}^{(l)}-\left\langle\bar{x}_{i}^{(l)}\bar{x}_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle, $$

when this functional is applied to another independent replica $\bar{\mathbf{x}}$ . With this notion, we can simplify $\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\lambda^{(l_{1})}\partial\lambda^{(l_{2})}}F_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})$ to

$$ \frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\lambda^{(l_{1})}\partial\lambda^{(l_{2})}}F_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=\frac{1}{2n^{3}}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i_{1}<j_{1}}\sum_{i_{2}<j_{2}}\left\langle\xi_{i_{1},j_{1}}^{(l_{1})}\xi_{i_{2},j_{2}}^{(l_{2})}\bar{\xi}_{i_{1},j_{1}}^{(l_{1})}\bar{\xi}_{i_{2},j_{2}}^{(l_{2})}\right\rangle\right]. $$

For any $(m_{1},\ldots,m_{L})\in\mathbb{R}^{L}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{l_{1},l_{2}}m_{l_{1}}m_{l_{2}}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\lambda^{(l_{1})}\partial\lambda^{(l_{2})}}F_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=\frac{1}{2n^{3}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle\left(\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{i<j}m_{l}\xi_{i,j}^{(l)}\bar{\xi}_{i,j}^{(l)}\right)^{2}\right\rangle\right]\geq 0. $$

In conclusion, $F_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})$ is jointly convex in $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ . Using Proposition 1.1, this series of multivariate convex functions converge pointwise to function

$$ \boldsymbol{\lambda}\mapsto\frac{\sum_{l}\lambda^{(l)}}{4}+\sup_{\mathbf{q}\geq 0}\left[\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{\lambda},\mathbf{q})-\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}(q_{l}^{2}+2q_{l})}{4}\right], $$

as $n\rightarrow\infty$ . Thus the limiting function is also convex. Set

$$ D=\left\{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in[0,\infty)^{L}:\sup_{\mathbf{q}\geq 0}\left[\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{\lambda},\mathbf{q})-\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}(q_{l}^{2}+2q_{l})}{4}\right]\text{ is not differentiable at }\boldsymbol{\lambda}\right\}. $$

Theorem 6.7(i) in Evans (2018) implies that every multivariate convex function is locally Lipschitz on an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^{L}$ . Using Rademacher’s Theorem (Theorem 3.1 or Theorem 6.6 in Evans (2018)), we have that any locally Lipschitz function is differentiable almost everywhere. Thus the set $D\subset[0,\infty)^{L}$ of bad points is of Lebesgue measure zero. Define $\boldsymbol{\gamma}=\left(\lambda^{(1)}q_{1},\ldots,\lambda^{(L)}q_{L}\right)$ , then we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{\mathbf{q}\geq 0}\left[\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{\lambda},\mathbf{q})-\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}(q_{l}^{2}+2q_{l})}{4}\right]=\sup_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}\geq 0}\left[-\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\gamma_{l}^{2}}{4\lambda^{(l)}}+\bar{\mathcal{F}}(\boldsymbol{\gamma})\right], \displaystyle\bar{\mathcal{F}}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}):=\mathbb{E} \displaystyle\log\left(\sum_{x,y}p(x,y|Z)e^{\sum_{l=1}^{L}\gamma_{l}X^{(l)}x^{(l)}+\sqrt{\gamma_{l}}W^{(l)\prime}x^{(l)}}\right)-\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\gamma_{l}}{2}=\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{\lambda},\mathbf{q})-\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}q_{l}}{2}. $$

It is easy to see that $\partial_{\gamma_{l}}\bar{\mathcal{F}}(\boldsymbol{\gamma})\leq 1/2<\gamma_{l}/(2\lambda^{(l)})$ if $\gamma_{l}>\lambda^{(l)}$ , so we can restrict the domain $\boldsymbol{\gamma}\geq 0$ of RHS in (4.3) onto a compact subset $\boldsymbol{\gamma}\in[0,\lambda^{(1)}]\times\cdots\times[0,\lambda^{(L)}]$ , thus enabling the use of envelope theorems, Milgrom and Segal (2002). For each $l\in[L]$ , apply the last argument (Milgrom and Segal, 2002, Corollary 4) on the functional

$$ G:(\lambda^{(l)},\boldsymbol{\gamma})\mapsto-\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\gamma_{l}^{2}}{4\lambda^{(l)}}+\bar{\mathcal{F}}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}), $$

to conclude: for $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ such that $\sup_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}G(\lambda^{(l)},\boldsymbol{\gamma})$ is differentiable in $\lambda^{(l)}$ , there exists a unique maximizer $\boldsymbol{\gamma}^{\ast}$ to $\sup_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}G(\lambda^{(l)},\boldsymbol{\gamma})$ and

$$ \frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda^{(l)}}\left[\sup_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}G(\lambda^{(l)},\boldsymbol{\gamma})\right]=\frac{\partial G}{\partial\lambda^{(l)}}(\lambda^{(l)},\boldsymbol{\gamma}^{\ast})=\frac{\left(\gamma^{\ast}_{l}\right)^{2}}{4\lambda^{(l)2}}. $$

Equivalently, we conclude that for any $\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in D^{c}$ , there exists a unique solution $\mathbf{q}^{\ast}$ to the maximization problem in functional (4.2) and its derivative is given by

$$ \frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda^{(l)}}\left[\sup_{\mathbf{q}\geq 0}\left[\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{\lambda},\mathbf{q})-\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}(q_{l}^{2}+2q_{l})}{4}\right]\right]=\frac{\left(q^{\ast}_{l}\right)^{2}}{4}. $$

The next display provides a direct relation connecting the minimal mean squared error to first-order derivatives $\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda^{(l)}}F_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{MMSE}\left(\mathbf{X}^{(l)};\mathbf{A},\mathbf{Z}\right)= \displaystyle\frac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i<j}\mathbb{E}\left(X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}-\mathbb{E}\left[X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}|\mathbf{A},\mathbf{Z}\right]\right)^{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i<j}\left[1-\mathbb{E}\left\langle X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle 1-\frac{2}{n(n-1)}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i<j}\left\langle X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle 2-\frac{4n}{n-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda^{(l)}}F_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda}). $$

If $\boldsymbol{\lambda}\notin D$ , the univariate function $\lambda^{(l)}\mapsto\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}F_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})$ is differentiable at $\lambda^{(l)}$ . By convexity in $\lambda^{(l)}$ and pointwise convergence of $F_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})$ , one can derive the convergence of first-order derivatives,

$$ \frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda^{(l)}}F_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda^{(l)}}\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}F_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda^{(l)}}\left\{\frac{\sum_{l}\lambda^{(l)}}{4}+\sup_{\mathbf{q}\geq 0}\left[\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{\lambda},\mathbf{q})-\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}(q_{l}^{2}+2q_{l})}{4}\right]\right\}. $$

Using (4.4) we conclude

$$ \mathsf{MMSE}\left(\mathbf{X}^{(l)};\mathbf{A},\mathbf{Z}\right)\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}1-\left(q^{\ast}_{l}\right)^{2},\quad\forall l\in[L] $$

for all $\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in D^{c}$ . ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 1.1 (iii).

We turn to optimal estimation of the implicit memberships $\mathbf{Y}^{(l_{1})}$ , $l_{1}\in[L_{1}]$ in this part. Fix $\lambda^{y}\geq 0$ and assume that we observe an additional spiked matrix of the form

$$ \mathbf{A}^{y}=\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{y}}{n}}\mathbf{Y}^{(l_{1})}\mathbf{Y}^{(l_{1})\top}+\mathbf{W}^{y}, $$

where $\mathbf{W}^{y}$ is another independent GOE. Our framework can incorporate this additional observation, and thus for any $(\lambda^{y},\boldsymbol{\lambda})\in[0,\infty)^{L+1}$ , (4.1) implies the conditional mutual information converges to

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{A},\mathbf{A}^{y}|\mathbf{Z})\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal{I}(\lambda^{y},\boldsymbol{\lambda}), $$

with limiting functional given by

$$ \mathcal{I}(\lambda^{y},\boldsymbol{\lambda})=\frac{\lambda^{y}+\sum_{l}\lambda^{(l)}}{4}-\sup_{q_{y},\mathbf{q}\geq 0}\left[\mathcal{F}(\lambda^{y},\boldsymbol{\lambda},q^{y},\mathbf{q})-\frac{\lambda^{y}(q_{y}^{2}+2q_{y})}{4}-\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}(q_{l}^{2}+2q_{l})}{4}\right], $$

where the augmented free energy functional is defined as

$$ \mathcal{F}(\lambda^{y},\boldsymbol{\lambda},q^{y},\mathbf{q})=\mathbb{E}\log\left(\sum_{x,y}p(x,y|Z)e^{\lambda^{y}q_{y}Y^{(l_{1})}y^{(l_{1})}+\sqrt{\lambda^{y}q_{y}}W^{\prime}y^{(l_{1})}+\sum_{l=1}^{L}\lambda^{(l)}q_{l}X^{(l)}x^{(l)}+\sqrt{\lambda^{(l)}q_{l}}W^{(l)\prime}x^{(l)}}\right). $$

We fix $\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in(0,\infty)^{L}\backslash D$ and vary $\lambda^{y}$ . Since $\mathcal{I}(\lambda^{y},\boldsymbol{\lambda})$ is concave in $\lambda^{y}\in[0,\infty)$ , there exists be a countable set $D^{y}\subset\mathbb{R}$ such that $\mathcal{I}(\lambda^{y},\boldsymbol{\lambda})$ is continuously differentiable in $\lambda^{y}\in(0,\infty)\backslash D^{y}$ . Using the envelope theorem (Milgrom and Segal, 2002, Corollary 4) for $\lambda^{y}\in(0,\infty)\backslash D^{y}$ , there exists a unique maximizer $(q_{y}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y}),\mathbf{q}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y}))\in\mathbb{R}^{L+1}$ and it satisfies

$$ \mathsf{MMSE}\left(\mathbf{Y}^{(l_{1})};\mathbf{A},\mathbf{A}^{y},\mathbf{Z}\right)\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}1-q^{\ast}_{y}\left(\lambda^{y}\right)^{2}. $$

#### Lemma 4.1.

Suppose $\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in[0,\infty)^{L}\backslash D$ is fixed and denote the associated unique maximizer $\mathbf{q}^{\ast}\in[0,\infty)^{L}$ (in the model without the augmented imaginary observation $\mathbf{A}^{y}$ in (4.5)). As $\lambda^{y}\in(0,\infty)\backslash D^{y}$ and $\lambda^{y}\rightarrow 0$ , we have

$$ q_{y}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y})\rightarrow\mathbb{E}\left[Y^{(l_{1})}\mathbb{E}\left(Y^{(l_{1})}|\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\odot\mathbf{q}^{\ast}}\odot X+W^{\prime}\right)\right]. $$

#### Proof.

For $\lambda^{y}\in(0,\infty)\backslash D^{y}$ and $\lambda^{y}\rightarrow 0$ , maximizers $(q_{y}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y}),\mathbf{q}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y}))$ are monotonic in $\lambda^{y}$ and bounded, therefore having a finite limit. The last assertion of Proposition 2.1 implies $(q_{y}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y}),\mathbf{q}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y}))$ satisfies a set of fixed point conditions,

$$ \displaystyle q_{y}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[Y^{(l_{1})}\mathbb{E}\left(Y^{(l_{1})}\big|\sqrt{\lambda^{y}q_{y}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y})}Y^{(l_{1})}+W_{y}^{\prime},\quad\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\odot\mathbf{q}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y})}\odot X+W^{\prime}\right)\right], \displaystyle q_{l}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[X^{(l)}\mathbb{E}\left(X^{(l)}\big|\sqrt{\lambda^{y}q_{y}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y})}Y^{(l_{1})}+W_{y}^{\prime},\quad\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\odot\mathbf{q}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y})}\odot X+W^{\prime}\right)\right],\quad l\in[L]. $$

The functional

$$ (\lambda^{y}q_{y},\lambda^{(1)}q_{1},\ldots,\lambda^{(L)}q_{L})\mapsto\mathbb{E}\left[X^{(l)}\mathbb{E}\left(X^{(l)}\big|\sqrt{\lambda^{y}q_{y}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y})}Y^{(l_{1})}+W_{y}^{\prime},\quad\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\odot\mathbf{q}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y})}\odot X+W^{\prime}\right)\right] $$

is smooth, so that the finite limit $\lim_{\lambda^{y}\rightarrow 0}\mathbf{q}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y})$ solves

$$ q_{l}=\mathbb{E}\left[X^{(l)}\mathbb{E}\left(X^{(l)}\big|\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\odot\mathbf{q}}\odot X+W^{\prime}\right)\right],\quad l\in[L]. $$

Recall that we set $\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in(0,\infty)^{L}\backslash D$ , so this equation set only has at most two solutions. Using continuity, we show that $\lim_{\lambda^{y}\rightarrow 0}\mathbf{q}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y})$ is a maximizer of the free energy functional. Therefore, we must have $\lim_{\lambda^{y}\rightarrow 0}\mathbf{q}^{\ast}(\lambda^{y})=\mathbf{q}^{\ast}$ . Lastly, take $\lambda^{y}\rightarrow 0$ in (4.7) to conclude the desired result. ∎

Equipped with this lemma, the lower bound of (1.14) is immediate,

$$ \displaystyle\quad\liminf_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathsf{MMSE}\left(\mathbf{Y}^{(l_{1})};\mathbf{A},\mathbf{Z}\right)\geq\lim_{\lambda^{y}\notin D^{y},\lambda^{y}\rightarrow 0^{+}}\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathsf{MMSE}\left(\mathbf{Y}^{(l_{1})};\mathbf{A},\mathbf{A}^{y},\mathbf{Z}\right) \displaystyle=\lim_{\lambda^{y}\notin D^{y},\lambda^{y}\rightarrow 0^{+}}\left[1-q^{\ast}_{y}\left(\lambda^{y}\right)^{2}\right]=1-\mathbb{E}\left[Y^{(l_{1})}\mathbb{E}\left(Y^{(l_{1})}|\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\odot\mathbf{q}^{\ast}}\odot X+W^{\prime}\right)\right]^{2}. $$

Next, we turn to a matching upper bound.

Step 1. The first step is to interpolate the additional side information $\mathbf{A}^{y}$ , similar to Section 3.1, finally deriving an upper bound on $\mathsf{MMSE}\left(\mathbf{Y}^{(l_{1})}\mathbf{Y}^{(l_{1})\top};\mathbf{A},\mathbf{Z}\right)$ . For some $\lambda^{y},q_{y}\geq 0$ and $t\in[0,1]$ to be determined, let’s focus on an observation model as this,

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &(X_{i},Y_{i},Z_{i})\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}p(\cdot),&1\leq i\leq n;\\
&A_{i,j}^{(l)}=\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}+W_{i,j}^{(l)},&1\leq i<j\leq n,1\leq l\leq L;\\
&A_{i,j}^{y}=\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{y}t}{n}}Y_{i}^{(l_{1})}Y_{j}^{(l_{1})\top}+W_{i,j}^{y},&1\leq i<j\leq n;\\
&Z^{\prime}_{i}=\sqrt{(1-t)\lambda^{y}q_{y}}Y_{i}+W^{\prime}_{i},&1\leq i\leq n,1\leq l\leq L;\end{aligned}\right. $$

with every $W$ being an independent standard normal. When $t=1$ , (4.8) corresponds to only adding additional observed matrix $\mathbf{A}^{y}$ ; when $t=0$ , it corresponds to only adding per-node side information $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}$ . Abbreviate normalized mutual information by

$$ \displaystyle\quad I_{n}(\lambda^{y},q_{y},t,\boldsymbol{\lambda}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{A},\mathbf{A}^{y},\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}|\mathbf{Z}) \displaystyle=\sum_{l}\frac{(n-1)\lambda^{(l)}}{2n}+\frac{(n-1)\lambda^{y}t}{2n}+(1-t)\lambda^{y}q_{y}-\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\log\left[\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}}p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{Z})H_{n}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},t)\right], $$

where the Hamiltonian $H_{n}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},t)$ is given by

$$ H_{n}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},t)=\sum_{l}\sum_{i<j}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}A_{i,j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}+\sum_{i<j}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{y}t}{n}}A^{y}_{i,j}y_{i}y_{j}+\sum_{i}\sqrt{(1-t)\lambda^{y}q_{y}}y_{i}Z_{i}^{\prime}. $$

Guerra’s interpolation technique, introduced in in Section 3.1, upper bounds the derivative of the mutual information with respect to $t$ by

$$ \frac{\partial}{\partial t}I_{n}(\lambda^{y},q_{y},t,\boldsymbol{\lambda})\leq\frac{\lambda^{y}}{4}-\frac{\lambda^{y}q_{y}}{2}+\frac{\lambda^{y}q_{y}^{2}}{4}. $$

Compared to the derivation in Section 3.1, a $o(1)$ term is made more explicit here as we want to derive a non-asymptotic upper bound. Therefore, the following holds for any $\lambda^{y},q_{y}\geq 0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle I_{n}(\lambda^{y},q_{y},1,\boldsymbol{\lambda}) \displaystyle=I_{n}(\lambda^{y},q_{y},0,\boldsymbol{\lambda})+\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}I_{n}(\lambda^{y},q_{y},t,\boldsymbol{\lambda})\mathrm{d}t \displaystyle\leq I_{n}(\lambda^{y},q_{y},0,\boldsymbol{\lambda})+\frac{\lambda^{y}}{4}-\frac{\lambda^{y}q_{y}}{2}+\frac{\lambda^{y}q_{y}^{2}}{4}. $$

As RHS equals LHS at $\lambda^{y}=0$ and they are both continuously differentiable at this boundary for any finite $n$ , it must hold for any $q_{y}\geq 0$ that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda^{y}}I_{n}(\lambda^{y},q_{y},1,\boldsymbol{\lambda})\Big|_{\lambda^{y}=0+} \displaystyle\leq\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda^{y}}I_{n}(\lambda^{y},q_{y},0,\boldsymbol{\lambda})\Big|_{\lambda^{y}=0+}+\frac{1}{4}(1-q_{y})^{2}. $$

When $t=1$ , differentiating with respect to $\lambda^{y}$ again gives the minimal mean squared error of $\mathbf{Y}^{(l_{1})}\mathbf{Y}^{(l_{1})\top}$ for any $\lambda^{y}\geq 0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda^{y}}I_{n}(\lambda^{y},q_{y},1,\boldsymbol{\lambda}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2(n-1)^{2}}\sum_{i<j}\left[1-\mathbb{E}\left\langle Y_{i}^{(l_{1})}Y_{j}^{(l_{1})}y_{i}^{(l_{1})}y_{j}^{(l_{1})}\right\rangle\right] \displaystyle=\frac{n}{4(n-1)}\mathsf{MMSE}\left(\mathbf{Y}^{(l_{1})};\mathbf{A},\mathbf{A}^{y},\mathbf{Z}\right). $$

When $t=0$ , differentiating with respect to $\lambda^{y}$ instead gives the minimal mean squared error of $\mathbf{Y}^{(l_{1})}$ for any $\lambda^{y}\geq 0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda^{y}}I_{n}(\lambda^{y},q_{y},0,\boldsymbol{\lambda}) \displaystyle=\frac{q_{y}}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[1-\mathbb{E}\left\langle Y_{i}^{(l_{1})}y_{i}^{(l_{1})}\right\rangle\right]. $$

Therefore, take $\lambda^{y}=0$ to derive

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{4}\mathsf{MMSE}\left(\mathbf{Y}^{(l_{1})}\mathbf{Y}^{(l_{1})\top};\mathbf{A},\mathbf{Z}\right) \displaystyle\leq\frac{q_{y}}{2}\mathsf{MMSE}\left(\mathbf{Y}^{(l_{1})};\mathbf{A},\mathbf{Z}\right)+\frac{1}{4}(1-q_{y})^{2} \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{4}+\frac{q_{y}^{2}}{4}-\frac{q_{y}}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{n}^{(l_{1})}\langle y_{n}^{(l_{1})}\rangle\right]. $$

Step 2. Our second step is to conduct a rigorous cavity computation as in Sections 3.3 and 3.4. Increasing $n$ to $n+1$ , we can decompose the Hamiltonian in the same way as Section 3.3,

$$ \displaystyle H_{n+1}(\mathbf{x},x_{n+1}) \displaystyle=H_{n}(\mathbf{x})-\delta(\mathbf{x})+\sum_{l=1}^{L}s_{l}(\mathbf{x})x_{n+1}^{(l)}, \displaystyle s_{l}(\mathbf{x}): \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n+1}x_{i}^{(l)}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{n+1}^{(l)}x_{n+1}^{(l)}+\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n+1}}W_{i,n+1}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{n+1}^{(l)}, $$

where $\mathbf{x}$ comprises the first $n$ elements and $s_{l}(\mathbf{x})$ is used to characterize how $\mathbf{x}$ influences $x_{n+1}$ , while

$$ \delta(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l)}n}{2(n+1)}\left(\mathbf{x}^{(l)}.\mathbf{X}^{(l)}\right)^{2}-\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{2(n+1)}+\sum_{i<j}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n(n+1)}}\widetilde{W}_{i,j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)} $$

is a term which adjusts changes in the denominator from $n$ to $n+1$ . We emphasize that $\langle\cdot\rangle_{n+1}$ (or $\langle\cdot\rangle_{n}$ resp.) is used to denote expectation over Gibbs distribution defined by Hamiltonian $H_{n+1}$ (or $H_{n}$ resp.). Continued from (4.9) in Step 1, we are interested at the following quantity

$$ \left\langle y^{(l_{1})}_{n+1}\right\rangle_{n+1}=\frac{\left\langle\sum_{x_{n+1},y_{n+1}}y^{(l_{1})}_{n+1}p(x_{n+1},y_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})\exp\left(-\delta(\mathbf{x})+\sum_{l}s_{l}(\mathbf{x})x_{n+1}^{(l)}\right)\right\rangle_{n}}{\left\langle\sum_{x_{n+1},y_{n+1}}p(x_{n+1},y_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})\exp\left(-\delta(\mathbf{x})+\sum_{l}s_{l}(\mathbf{x})x_{n+1}^{(l)}\right)\right\rangle_{n}}:=\frac{V_{1}}{U_{1}}. $$

#### Lemma 4.2.

For any $\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in(0,\infty)^{L}\backslash D$ , suppose $\mathbf{x},\bar{\mathbf{x}}$ are drawn independently from $\langle\cdot\rangle_{n}$ , then the following overlap concentration holds,

$$ \mathbb{E}\left\langle\left[\left(\mathbf{x}^{(l)}.\bar{\mathbf{x}}^{(l)}\right)^{2}-\left(q_{l}^{\ast}\right)^{2}\right]^{2}\right\rangle_{n}\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}0,\quad l\in[L]. $$

#### Proof.

In the process of proving the RS prediction on normalized free energy (Proposition 1.1), Section 3.2 shows the overlap to concentrate under a small perturbation defined in (3.8). In this case we start from Proposition 1.1 and thus we do not need to introduce the perturbation. The proof is essentially the same as Section 4 in Lelarge and Miolane (2019), which is an adaptation of the proof for Ghirlanda-Guerra identities from Section 3.7 in Panchenko (2013). ∎

Setting $q_{l,n}=\langle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{(l)}\bar{x}_{i}^{(l)}\rangle_{n}$ to denote the expected overlap, it follows that $\mathbb{E}\left|q_{l,n}-q^{\ast}\right|\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}0$ from Lemma 4.2. Building upon this intuition, $s_{l}(\mathbf{x})x_{n+1}^{(l)}$ will be well approximated by $s_{l}^{0}x_{n+1}^{(l)}+\frac{\lambda^{(l)}-\lambda^{(l)}q_{l,n}}{2}$ where

$$ s_{l}^{0}:=\lambda^{(l)}q_{l,n}X_{n+1}^{(l)}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}W_{i,n+1}^{(l)}\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)}\right\rangle_{n}. $$

In addition, $\delta(\mathbf{x})$ will be approximated by

$$ \delta^{0}:=\sum_{l=1}^{L}\left[\frac{\lambda^{(l)}q_{l,n}^{2}+\lambda^{(l)}}{4}+\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}\frac{\sqrt{\lambda^{(l)}}}{n}\widetilde{W}_{i,j}^{(l)}\left\langle x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\rangle_{n}\right]. $$

Replacing $(\delta,s_{l})$ by their respective mean-field surrogates, we define

$$ \displaystyle U_{2}= \displaystyle\sum_{x_{n+1},y_{n+1}}p(x_{n+1},y_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})e^{-\delta^{0}+\sum_{l}s_{l}^{0}x_{n+1}^{(l)}+\frac{\lambda^{(l)}-\lambda^{(l)}q_{l,n}}{2}}, \displaystyle V_{2}= \displaystyle\sum_{x_{n+1},y_{n+1}}y_{n+1}^{(l_{1})}p(x_{n+1},y_{n+1}|Z_{n+1})e^{-\delta^{0}+\sum_{l}s_{l}^{0}x_{n+1}^{(l)}+\frac{\lambda^{(l)}-\lambda^{(l)}q_{l,n}}{2}}. $$

Using Lemma 4.2, we can repeat the arguments in the proof of Lemma 3.4 to derive

$$ \mathbb{E}\left|U_{1}-U_{2}\right|^{2}\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}0,\quad\mathbb{E}\left|V_{1}-V_{2}\right|^{2}\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}0. $$

In addition, repeating Lemma 3.5, we also have $\mathbb{E}U_{1}^{-2}+\mathbb{E}U_{2}^{-2}\leq C$ for some $C>0$ independent of $n$ . Note that by definition, $|V_{1}/U_{1}|=\left|\left\langle y^{(l_{1})}_{n+1}\right\rangle_{n+1}\right|\leq 1$ . Thus we have,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left|\frac{V_{1}}{U_{1}}-\frac{V_{2}}{U_{2}}\right| \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{V_{1}}{U_{1}}U_{2}^{-1}\left|U_{1}-U_{2}\right|\right]+\mathbb{E}U_{2}^{-1}\left|V_{1}-V_{2}\right| \displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}U_{2}^{-2}}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left|U_{1}-U_{2}\right|^{2}}+\sqrt{\mathbb{E}U_{2}^{-2}}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left|V_{1}-V_{2}\right|^{2}}\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}0, $$

which implies $\left|\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{n+1}^{(l_{1})}\langle y_{n+1}^{(l_{1})}\rangle\right]-\mathbb{E}Y_{n+1}^{(l_{1})}V_{2}/U_{2}\right|\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}0$ . Lastly, since $\mathbb{E}\left|q_{l,n}-q^{\ast}_{l}\right|\rightarrow 0$ , we conclude

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[Y_{n+1}^{(l_{1})}\langle y_{n+1}^{(l_{1})}\rangle\right]\rightarrow\mathbb{E}\left[Y^{(l)}\mathbb{E}\left(Y^{(l_{1})}|Z,\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\odot\mathbf{q}^{\ast}}\odot X+W^{\prime}\right)\right]. $$

Consequently, using (4.9) we have,

$$ \limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathsf{MMSE}\left(\mathbf{Y}^{(l_{1})};\mathbf{A},\mathbf{Z}\right)\leq\frac{1}{4}+\frac{q_{y}^{2}}{4}-\frac{q_{y}}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[Y^{(l)}\mathbb{E}\left(Y^{(l_{1})}|Z,\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\odot\mathbf{q}^{\ast}}\odot X+W^{\prime}\right)\right]. $$

Finally, we set $q_{y}=\mathbb{E}\left[Y^{(l)}\mathbb{E}\left(Y^{(l_{1})}|Z,\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\odot\mathbf{q}^{\ast}}\odot X+W^{\prime}\right)\right]$ to conclude the proof. ∎

### 4.2 Universality of Mutual Information

We turn to a proof of Proposition 1.2 in this section. Since $I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{G},\mathbf{Z})$ (resp. $I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{A},\mathbf{Z})$ ) always differs from $I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{G}\mid\mathbf{Z})$ (resp. $I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{A}\mid\mathbf{Z})$ ) with a fixed term $ni_{p}(x,y;z)$ , it suffices to control the difference between the conditional mutual information in the graph problem (with finite $d_{n}$ ) and the mutual information in the spiked gaussian matrix problem.

#### Proposition 4.1.

Under the asymptotics that (i) $\lambda^{(l)}_{n}\rightarrow\lambda^{(l)}$ for any $l\in[L]$ and (ii) $\min_{l}d^{(l)}(1-d^{(l)}/n)\rightarrow\infty$ , the following universality result holds in terms of mutual information for the graph model (1.1) and its spiked matrix counterpart (1.6),

$$ \left|\frac{1}{n}I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{G}\mid\mathbf{Z})-\frac{1}{n}I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{A}\mid\mathbf{Z})\right|\leq O\left(\sum_{l}|\lambda^{(l)}_{n}-\lambda^{(l)}|+\sum_{l}\frac{(\lambda^{(l)})^{3/2}}{\sqrt{d^{(l)}(1-d^{(l)}/n)}}\right). $$

Our proof strategy mirrors the one used in (Deshpande et al., 2017, Proposition 4.1) and (Lelarge and Miolane, 2019, Theorem 54). To establish this proposition, we need two intermediate lemmas. To this end, let

$$ \tau_{l}=\frac{a^{(l)}-b^{(l)}}{a^{(l)}+b^{(l)}}=\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}_{n}(1-d^{(l)}/n)}{d^{(l)}}} $$

measure the discrepency of in-community connectivity and cross-community connectivity for layer $l$ . For any $i<j,l\in[L]$ , define

$$ D_{i,j}^{(l)}:=\frac{\tau_{l}}{1-d^{(l)}/n}\left(G_{i,j}^{(l)}-\mathbb{E}\left[G_{i,j}^{(l)}\mid\mathbf{X}\right]\right)=\frac{\tau_{l}}{1-d^{(l)}/n}\left(G_{i,j}^{(l)}-\frac{d^{(l)}}{n}-\frac{d^{(l)}\tau_{l}}{n}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}\right). $$

Our first lemma simplifies the definition of $I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{G}|\mathbf{Z})$ via Taylor expansion.

#### Lemma 4.3.

Under the same asymptotics as Proposition 4.1, the conditional mutual information $I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{G}|\mathbf{Z})$ can be approximated by

$$ \displaystyle J_{1}=-\mathbb{E}\log\left[\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}}p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{Z})e^{\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{i<j}D_{i,j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}+\frac{\lambda^{(l)}_{n}}{n}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}-\frac{\lambda^{(l)}_{n}}{n}}\right]. $$

in the sense that

$$ \limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n}\left|J_{1}-I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{G}|\mathbf{Z})\right|\leq O\left(\sum_{l}\frac{(\lambda^{(l)})^{3/2}}{\sqrt{d^{(l)}(1-d^{(l)}/n)}}\right). $$

Recall now the definition of $I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{A}|\mathbf{Z})$ ,

$$ I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{A}|\mathbf{Z})=-\mathbb{E}\log\left[\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}}p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{Z})e^{\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{i<j}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}W_{i,j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}+\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}-\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}\right]. $$

By direct comparison, we find that $J_{1}$ differs from $I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{A}|\mathbf{Z})$ by replacing $\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}W_{i,j}^{(l)}$ by $D_{i,j}^{(l)}$ and $\lambda^{(l)}$ by $\lambda^{(l)}_{n}$ . Our next lemma uses Lindeberg swapping to show that this change is asymptotically negligible.

#### Lemma 4.4.

Under the same asymptotics as Proposition 4.1, we have

$$ \limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n}\left|J_{1}-I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{A}|\mathbf{Z})\right|\leq O\left(\sum_{l}|\lambda^{(l)}_{n}-\lambda^{(l)}|+\frac{(\lambda^{(l)})^{3/2}}{\sqrt{d^{(l)}(1-d^{(l)}/n)}}\right). $$

Proposition 4.1 directly follows from combining Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4.

#### Taylor Expansion of Bernoulli p.m.f.

We start with a Chernoff-style bound on the upper tail of the total number of edges. The proof is standard, and thus omitted.

#### Proof of Lemma 4.3.

By definition, $I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{G}|\mathbf{Z})=-\mathbb{E}\log\frac{p(\mathbf{G}|\mathbf{Z})}{p(\mathbf{G}\mid\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z})}$ . Thus

$$ I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{G}|\mathbf{Z})=-\mathbb{E}\log\frac{\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}}p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{Z})p(\mathbf{G}|\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})}{p(\mathbf{G}\mid\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})}. $$

Recall that $p(\mathbf{G}|\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\prod_{l}p(\mathbf{G}^{(l)}|\mathbf{x}^{(l)},\mathbf{y}^{(l)})$ with

$$ \displaystyle p(\mathbf{G}^{(l)}|\mathbf{x}^{(l)},\mathbf{y}^{(l)})=\prod_{i<j}M(x_{i}^{(l)},x_{j}^{(l)})^{G_{i,j}^{(l)}}\left(1-M(x_{i}^{(l)},x_{j}^{(l)})\right)^{1-G_{i,j}^{(l)}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\exp\left[\sum_{i<j}G_{i,j}^{(l)}\log M(x_{i}^{(l)},x_{j}^{(l)})+\left(1-G_{i,j}^{(l)}\right)\log\left(1-M(x_{i}^{(l)},x_{j}^{(l)})\right)\right] $$

where we set $M(x_{i}^{(l)},x_{j}^{(l)})=\frac{d^{(l)}}{n}\left(1+x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\tau_{l}\right)$ . Equipped with this notation,

$$ \displaystyle I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{G}|\mathbf{Z})=-\mathbb{E}\log\Bigg[\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}}p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{Z})\exp\Bigg(\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{i<j} \displaystyle G_{i,j}^{(l)}\log\left(\frac{M(x_{i}^{(l)},x_{j}^{(l)})}{M(X_{i}^{(l)},X_{j}^{(l)})}\right) \displaystyle+\left(1-G_{i,j}^{(l)}\right)\log\left(\frac{1-M(x_{i}^{(l)},x_{j}^{(l)})}{1-M(X_{i}^{(l)},X_{j}^{(l)})}\right)\Bigg)\Bigg]. $$

Note that $\log\left(\frac{M(x_{i}^{(l)},x_{j}^{(l)})}{M(X_{i}^{(l)},X_{j}^{(l)})}\right)=\log\left(\frac{1+x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\tau_{l}}{1+X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}\tau_{l}}\right)$ . By the Taylor-Lagrange inequality, there exists a universal constant $C>0$ such that, for $\tau_{l}$ small enough (i.e. for $d$ large enough),

$$ \displaystyle\left|\log\left(\frac{1+x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\tau_{l}}{1+X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}\tau_{l}}\right)-\tau_{l}\left(x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}-X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}\right)\right|\leq C\tau_{l}^{3}. $$

Moreover, since $\log(c+dx)=\frac{1}{2}\log\left((c+d)(c-d)\right)+\frac{x}{2}\log\frac{c+d}{c-d}$ for any $x\in\{\pm 1\}$ , we find

$$ \displaystyle\log\left(\frac{1-M(x_{i}^{(l)},x_{j}^{(l)})}{1-M(X_{i}^{(l)},X_{j}^{(l)})}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left(x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}-X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}\right)\log\frac{1-d^{(l)}/n-\tau_{l}d^{(l)}/n}{1-d^{(l)}/n+\tau_{l}d^{(l)}/n}. $$

Taylor expansion also implies $\left|\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{1+z}{1-z}\right)-z\right|\leq z^{3}$ , which further deduces

$$ \displaystyle\left|\log\left(\frac{1-M(x_{i}^{(l)},x_{j}^{(l)})}{1-M(X_{i}^{(l)},X_{j}^{(l)})}\right)+\frac{\tau_{l}d^{(l)}/n}{1-d^{(l)}/n}\left(x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}-X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}\right)\right|\leq C\left(\frac{\tau_{l}d^{(l)}/n}{1-d^{(l)}/n}\right)^{3}. $$

Summing over $i<j$ and using triangle inequality, we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i<j}G_{i,j}^{(l)}\log\left(\frac{M(x_{i}^{(l)},x_{j}^{(l)})}{M(X_{i}^{(l)},X_{j}^{(l)})}\right)+\left(1-G_{i,j}^{(l)}\right)\log\left(\frac{1-M(x_{i}^{(l)},x_{j}^{(l)})}{1-M(X_{i}^{(l)},X_{j}^{(l)})}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{i<j}\left(\tau_{l}\left(x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}-X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}\right)G_{i,j}^{(l)}-\left(1-G_{i,j}^{(l)}\right)\left(x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}-X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}\right)\frac{\tau_{l}d^{(l)}/n}{1-d^{(l)}/n}\right)+\Delta_{n}^{(l)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{i<j}\frac{\tau_{l}}{1-d^{(l)}/n}\left(x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}-X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}\right)\left(G_{i,j}^{(l)}-\frac{d^{(l)}}{n}\right)+\Delta_{n}^{(l)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{i<j}\left(\left(x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}-X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}\right)D_{i,j}^{(l)}+\frac{\lambda^{(l)}_{n}}{n}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}-\frac{\lambda^{(l)}_{n}}{n}\right)+\Delta_{n}^{(l)}, $$

where $\Delta_{n}^{(l)}$ is a residual term satisfying

$$ \left|\Delta_{n}^{(l)}\right|\leq C\left[\sum_{i<j}G_{i,j}^{(l)}\tau_{l}^{3}+(1-G_{i,j}^{(l)})\left(\frac{\tau_{l}d^{(l)}/n}{1-d^{(l)}/n}\right)^{3}\right], $$

where $C>0$ is a universal constant. Consequently, we can express

$$ \displaystyle I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{G}|\mathbf{Z})= \displaystyle-\mathbb{E}\log\Bigg[\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}}p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{Z})\exp\Bigg(\Delta_{n}^{(l)} \displaystyle+\sum_{l}\sum_{i<j}\left(\left(x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}-X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}\right)D_{i,j}^{(l)}+\frac{\lambda^{(l)}_{n}}{n}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}-\frac{\lambda^{(l)}_{n}}{n}\right.\Bigg)\Bigg]. $$

Define $\mathsf{err}=I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{G}|\mathbf{Z})-J_{1}$ with $J_{1}$ from (4.12). For any fixed realization $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{G})$ , error term $\left|\Delta_{n}^{(l)}\right|$ has a uniform upper bound as shown in (4.16) for any possible $(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$ , so it follows that

$$ \displaystyle|\mathsf{err}| \displaystyle\leq C\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{l}\sum_{i<j}G_{i,j}^{(l)}\tau_{l}^{3}+(1-G_{i,j}^{(l)})\left(\frac{\tau_{l}d^{(l)}/n}{1-d^{(l)}/n}\right)^{3}\right], \displaystyle\leq O\left(\sum_{l}\tau_{l}^{3}\mathbb{E}\sum_{i<j}G_{i,j}^{(l)}\right)+O\left(\sum_{l}\left(\frac{\tau_{l}d^{(l)}/n}{1-d^{(l)}/n}\right)^{3}\mathbb{E}\sum_{i<j}(1-G_{i,j}^{(l)})\right) \displaystyle\leq O\left(\sum_{l}\frac{n(\lambda^{(l)}_{n})^{3/2}(1-d^{(l)}/n)^{3/2}}{\sqrt{d^{(l)}}}\right)+O\left(\sum_{l}\frac{(\lambda^{(l)}_{n})^{3/2}(d^{(l)})^{3/2}}{n\sqrt{1-d^{(l)}/n}}\right) \displaystyle\leq O\left(n\sum_{l}\frac{(\lambda^{(l)})^{3/2}}{\sqrt{d^{(l)}(1-d^{(l)}/n)}}\right). $$

where the third inequality uses the direct fact that,

$$ \mathbb{E}\sum_{i<j}G_{i,j}^{(l)}\leq Cnd^{(l)},\quad\mathbb{E}\sum_{i<j}\left(1-G_{i,j}^{(l)}\right)\leq Cn^{2}(1-d^{(l)}/n); $$

while the final inequality uses $\lambda^{(l)}_{n}\rightarrow\lambda^{(l)}$ , $d^{(l)}\leq n$ and $1-d^{(l)}/n\leq 1$ . Until this end, we can conclude Lemma 4.3. ∎

#### Lindeberg Exchange

The following generalization of Lindeberg’s theorem is adapted from (Korada and Montanari, 2011, Theorem 2).

#### Lemma 4.5 (Korada and Montanari (2011)).

Let $\left(U_{i}\right)_{1\leq i\leq n}$ and $\left(V_{i}\right)_{1\leq i\leq n}$ be two collection of random variables with independent components and $f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ a $\mathcal{C}^{3}$ function. Denote $a_{i}=\left|\mathbb{E}U_{i}-\mathbb{E}V_{i}\right|$ and $b_{i}=\left|\mathbb{E}U_{i}^{2}-\mathbb{E}V_{i}^{2}\right|$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle|\mathbb{E}f(U)-\mathbb{E}f(V)|\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(a_{i}\mathbb{E}\left|\partial_{i}f\left(U_{1:i-1},0,V_{i+1:n}\right)\right|+\frac{b_{i}}{2}\mathbb{E}\left|\partial_{i}^{2}f\left(U_{1:i-1},0,V_{i+1:n}\right)\right|\right. \displaystyle\left.+\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{U_{i}}\left|\partial_{i}^{3}f\left(U_{1:i-1},0,V_{i+1:n}\right)\right|\left(U_{i}-s\right)^{2}ds+\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{V_{i}}\left|\partial_{i}^{3}f\left(U_{1:i-1},0,V_{i+1:n}\right)\right|\left(V_{i}-s\right)^{2}ds\right). $$

#### Proof of Lemma 4.4.

Conditioned on $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z})$ , introduce the following function

$$ \Phi(\mathbf{u},\boldsymbol{\lambda})=-\log\left[\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}}p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{Z})e^{\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{i<j}u_{i,j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}+\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}X_{i}^{(l)}X_{j}^{(l)}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}-\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}\right] $$

for each aggregation $\mathbf{u}=\left\{u_{i,j}^{(l)}:l\in[L],i<j\right\}$ and $\boldsymbol{\lambda}=\left\{\lambda^{(l)}:l\in[L]\right\}$ . Function $\Phi(\mathbf{u},\boldsymbol{\lambda})$ is thus $\mathcal{C}^{3}$ in $\mathbf{u}$ with bounded derivatives since the support of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{x}$ are bounded. Notice that $J_{1}=\mathbb{E}\Phi(\mathbf{D},\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{n})$ and $I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{A}|\mathbf{Z})=\mathbb{E}\Phi\left(\sqrt{\frac{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}{n}}\mathbf{W},\boldsymbol{\lambda}\right)$ . We then proceed to compute the moments of $D_{i,j}^{(l)}$ whose definition is from (4.11), conditionally to $\mathbf{X}$ . Firstly, $D_{i,j}^{(l)}$ is also of mean zero like $\sqrt{\lambda^{(l)}/n}W_{i,j}^{(l)}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{E}\left(D_{i,j}^{(l)}\mid\mathbf{X}\right)=\mathbb{E}\left(\sqrt{\lambda^{(l)}/n}W_{i,j}^{(l)}\right)=0. $$

Secondly, its second moment can be computed as

$$ \displaystyle\quad\mathbb{E}\left(D_{i,j}^{(l)2}\mid\mathbf{X}\right)=\frac{\tau_{l}^{2}}{(1-d^{(l)}/n)^{2}}\operatorname{Var}\left(G_{i,j}^{(l)}\mid\mathbf{X}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{\lambda^{(l)}_{n}/n}{d^{(l)}(1-d^{(l)}/n)}\left[a^{(l)}(1-a^{(l)}/n)\mathbbm{1}\{X_{i}^{(l)}=X_{j}^{(l)}\}+b^{(l)}(1-b^{(l)}/n)\mathbbm{1}\{X_{i}^{(l)}\neq X_{j}^{(l)}\}\right], $$

while $\mathbb{E}\left(\sqrt{\lambda^{(l)}/n}W_{i,j}^{(l)}\right)^{2}=\lambda^{(l)}/n$ . Under the asymptotics that (i) $\lambda^{(l)}_{n}\rightarrow\lambda^{(l)}$ for any $l\in[L]$ and (ii) $\min_{l}d^{(l)}(1-d^{(l)}/n)\rightarrow\infty$ , we have

$$ \left|\frac{a^{(l)}(1-a^{(l)}/n)}{d^{(l)}(1-d^{(l)}/n)}-1\right|\leq C\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{d^{(l)}(1-d^{(l)}/n)}}; $$

and the same holds as well when $a^{(l)}$ is replaced by $b^{(l)}$ . Consequently, differences in the second moments can be controlled by

$$ \left|\mathbb{E}\left(D_{i,j}^{(l)2}\mid\mathbf{X}\right)-\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}\right|\leq\frac{|\lambda^{(l)}_{n}-\lambda^{(l)}|}{n}+\frac{C}{n}\frac{(\lambda^{(l)})^{3/2}}{\sqrt{d^{(l)}(1-d^{(l)}/n)}}. $$

The third moments is also bounded by $\mathbb{E}\left(D_{i,j}^{(l)3}\mid\mathbf{X}\right)=O\left(\frac{1}{n}\frac{(\lambda^{(l)})^{3/2}}{\sqrt{d^{(l)}(1-d^{(l)}/n)}}\right)$ . From Lemma 4.5 we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\quad\left|J_{1}-\mathbb{E}\Phi\left(\sqrt{\frac{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}{n}}\mathbf{W},\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{n}\right)\right|=\left|\mathbb{E}\Phi\left(\mathbf{D},\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{n}\right)-\mathbb{E}\Phi\left(\sqrt{\frac{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}{n}}\mathbf{W},\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{n}\right)\right| \displaystyle\leq\sum_{l}\sum_{i<j}O\left(\frac{|\lambda^{(l)}_{n}-\lambda^{(l)}|}{n}+\frac{1}{n}\frac{(\lambda^{(l)})^{3/2}}{\sqrt{d^{(l)}(1-d^{(l)}/n)}}\right) \displaystyle=O\left(n\sum_{l}|\lambda^{(l)}_{n}-\lambda^{(l)}|+n\sum_{l}\frac{(\lambda^{(l)})^{3/2}}{\sqrt{d^{(l)}(1-d^{(l)}/n)}}\right). $$

The last step is to note that $|\partial_{\lambda^{(l)}}\Phi(\mathbf{u},\boldsymbol{\lambda})|\leq Cn$ always holds for some universal constant $C>0$ since $\mathbf{X},\mathbf{x}$ are bounded. Followed by

$$ \left|\mathbb{E}\Phi\left(\sqrt{\frac{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}{n}}\mathbf{W},\boldsymbol{\lambda}\right)-\mathbb{E}\Phi\left(\sqrt{\frac{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}{n}}\mathbf{W},\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{n}\right)\right|\leq O\left(n\sum_{l}|\lambda^{(l)}_{n}-\lambda^{(l)}|\right), $$

Lemma 4.4 is finally established. ∎

### 4.3 Universality of Minimal MSE

We establish Proposition 1.3 in this section. To this end, the following lemma connects the graph models minimal MSE to the derivative of the mutual information.

#### Lemma 4.6.

There exists a universal constant $C>0$ such that: for any fixed $\lambda_{0}$ , there exists $n_{0}(\lambda_{0})$ such that for all $0<\lambda^{(l)}\leq\lambda_{0}$ , and $n\geq n_{0}(\lambda_{0})$ ,

$$ \left|\frac{1}{n}\frac{\partial I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{G}\mid\mathbf{Z})}{\partial\lambda^{(l)}}-\frac{1}{4}\mathsf{MMSE}\left(\mathbf{X}^{(l)}\mathbf{X}^{(l)\top};\mathbf{G},\mathbf{Z}\right)\right|\leq C\left(\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{d^{(l)}(1-d^{(l)}/n)}}\lor\frac{1}{n}\right). $$

This lemma is in the same spirit as (Deshpande et al., 2017, Lemma 7.2) and (Lelarge and Miolane, 2019, Proposition 62). Consequently, we omit the proof. In the following, to emphasize the dependence on $\lambda^{(l)}$ , we write

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{MMSE}_{l}^{\mathsf{G}}(\lambda^{(l)},n) \displaystyle=\mathsf{MMSE}\left(\mathbf{X}^{(l)}\mathbf{X}^{(l)\top};\mathbf{G},\mathbf{Z}\right), \displaystyle\Phi(\lambda^{(l)})=i_{p}(x,y;z)+ \displaystyle\frac{\sum_{l^{\prime}}\lambda^{(l^{\prime})}}{4}-\sup_{\mathbf{q}\geq 0}\left[\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{\lambda},\mathbf{q})-\sum_{l^{\prime}=1}^{L}\frac{\lambda^{(l^{\prime})}(q_{l^{\prime}}^{2}+2q_{l^{\prime}})}{4}\right], $$

where the last term appears in (1.12). As defined in (1.15), we are comparing $\mathsf{MMSE}_{l}(\lambda^{(l)})$ with the best possible estimate only from per-vertex side information $\mathbf{Z}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{DMSE}_{l}(p): \displaystyle=1-\left\{\mathbb{E}\left[X^{(l)}\mathbb{E}\left(X^{(l)}|Z\right)\right]\right\}^{2}, $$

which only depends on the prior $p$ and is irrelevant of $n$ . As the free energy is convex in $\lambda^{(l)}$ , using Theorem 1.1, for all but countably many $\lambda^{(l)}$ ,

$$ \Phi^{\prime}(\lambda^{(l)})=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{4}\mathsf{MMSE}\left(\mathbf{X}^{(l)}\mathbf{X}^{(l)\top};\mathbf{A},\mathbf{Z}\right). $$

Using Lemma 4.6, under the asymptotics that $\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{n}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ and $d^{(l)}(1-d^{(l)}/n)\rightarrow\infty$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\quad\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|\frac{1}{4}\int_{0}^{\lambda^{(l)}}\mathsf{MMSE}_{l}^{\mathsf{G}}(\lambda^{\prime},n)\mathrm{d}\lambda^{\prime}-\Phi(\lambda^{(l)})\right| \displaystyle\leq\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|\frac{1}{4}\int_{0}^{\lambda^{(l)}}\mathsf{MMSE}_{l}^{\mathsf{G}}(\lambda^{\prime},n)\mathrm{d}\lambda^{\prime}-\frac{1}{n}I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{G}\mid\mathbf{Z})\right|+\left|\frac{1}{n}I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{G}\mid\mathbf{Z})-\Phi(\lambda^{(l)})\right| \displaystyle\leq O\left(|\lambda^{(l)}_{n}-\lambda^{(l)}|+\frac{(\lambda^{(l)})^{3/2}}{\sqrt{d^{(l)}(1-d^{(l)}/n)}}\lor\frac{1}{n}\right), $$

where for last inequality we also use Proposition 1.2 to upper bound $\left|\frac{1}{n}I(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{G}\mid\mathbf{Z})-\Phi(\lambda^{(l)})\right|$ .

#### Proof of Proposition 1.3.

(i) If $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ is below the weak recovery threshold for the graph model, such that

$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathsf{MMSE}_{l}^{\mathsf{G}}(\lambda^{(l)},n)=\mathsf{DMSE}_{l}(p), $$

it follows from monotonicity that $\mathsf{MMSE}_{l}^{\mathsf{G}}(\lambda^{\prime},n)=\mathsf{DMSE}_{l}(p)$ remains constant for any $0\leq\lambda^{\prime}\leq\lambda^{(l)}$ . Thereafter, (4.17) deduces $\Phi(\lambda^{\prime})=\frac{\lambda^{\prime}}{4}\mathsf{DMSE}_{l}(p)$ to be linear in $0\leq\lambda^{\prime}\leq\lambda^{(l)}$ . It follows

$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{4}\mathsf{MMSE}\left(\mathbf{X}^{(l)}\mathbf{X}^{(l)\top};\mathbf{A},\mathbf{Z}\right)=\Phi^{\prime}(\lambda^{(l)})=\mathsf{DMSE}_{l}(p). $$

Consequently, $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ is also below the weak recovery threshold for the spiked matrix model. (ii) On the other hand, if $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ is above the weak recovery threshold for the graph model, such that

$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathsf{MMSE}_{l}^{\mathsf{G}}(\lambda^{(l)},n)<\mathsf{DMSE}_{l}(p). $$

We then proceed by contradiction. Suppose $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ is below the weak recovery threshold for the spiked matrix model, i.e.

$$ \limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathsf{MMSE}\left(\mathbf{X}^{(l)}\mathbf{X}^{(l)\top};\mathbf{A},\mathbf{Z}\right)=\mathsf{DMSE}_{l}(p). $$

By definition, we must know $\Phi(\lambda^{\prime})=\frac{\lambda^{\prime}}{4}\mathsf{DMSE}_{l}(p)$ to be linear in $0\leq\lambda^{\prime}\leq\lambda^{(l)}$ . But instead, (4.18) and (4.17) together suggest $\Phi(\lambda^{(l)})<\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{4}\mathsf{DMSE}_{l}(p)$ , resulting in a contradiction. Therefore, we must find $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ above the weak recovery threshold for the spiked matrix model. Combining these two assertions yields the weak recovery thresholds to be universal from spiked matrices to random graphs, thereby proving Proposition 1.3. ∎

## 5 Approximate Message Passing

We derive the AMP algorithm (Algorithm 1) in Section 5.1. Subsequently, we characterize the state evolution behavior of this algorithm in Section 5.2. Finally, we establish the universality of the AMP algorithm in Section 5.3.

### 5.1 Heuristic Derivations

To simplify notations, we omit the dependence of the posterior on $(\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A})$ for this subsection. Specifically, we use

$$ p_{i}(x_{i},y_{i}):=p(x_{i},y_{i}|Z_{i}), $$

and denote the joint posterior $p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{A})$ by

$$ \mu(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\propto\prod_{i}p_{i}(x_{i},y_{i})\cdot\exp\left\{\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}A^{(l)}_{i,j}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\}. $$

With a factorized base measure $\otimes_{i}p_{i}$ on $(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$ , the posterior is a Gibbs measure with Hamiltonian $H(\mathbf{x}):=\sum_{i<j}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}A^{(l)}_{i,j}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}$ .

We treat each $(x_{i},y_{i})$ jointly as a spin variable, and each marginal is denoted as $\mu_{i}$ . For any disjoint $A,B\subset[n]$ , we set $\nu_{A\rightarrow B}(\mathbf{x}_{A},\mathbf{y}_{A})$ as the marginal distribution of $(\mathbf{x}_{A},\mathbf{y}_{A})$ with $(\mathbf{x}_{B},\mathbf{y}_{B})$ removed. Due to the separability of $H(\mathbf{x})$ , we have,

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{i}\left(x_{i},y_{i}\right)/p_{i}(x_{i},y_{i}) \displaystyle\propto \displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{x}_{[n]\backslash i},\mathbf{y}_{[n]\backslash i}}\prod_{k\neq i}p_{i}(x_{k},y_{k})\cdot\exp\left\{\sum_{k<j:k,j\in[n]\backslash i}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}A^{(l)}_{k,j}x_{k}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}+\sum_{j\in[n]\backslash i}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}A^{(l)}_{i,j}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\} \displaystyle\propto \displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{x}_{[n]\backslash i},\mathbf{y}_{[n]\backslash i}}\nu_{[n]\backslash i\rightarrow i}(\mathbf{x}_{[n]\backslash i},\mathbf{y}_{[n]\backslash i})\cdot\exp\left\{\sum_{j\in[n]\backslash i}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}A^{(l)}_{i,j}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\}. $$

We invoke the replica symmetry assumption to continue our derivation : cavity distribution $\nu_{[n]\backslash i\rightarrow i}(\mathbf{x}_{[n]\backslash i},\mathbf{y}_{[n]\backslash i})$ is approximately independent across the spins, namely $\nu_{[n]\backslash i\rightarrow i}(\mathbf{x}_{[n]\backslash i},\mathbf{y}_{[n]\backslash i})=\prod_{j\in[n]\backslash i}\nu_{j\rightarrow i}(x_{j},y_{j})+o(1)$ . In turn, this implies

$$ \mu_{i}\left(x_{i},y_{i}\right)\propto p_{i}\left(x_{i},y_{i}\right)\sum_{\mathbf{x}_{[n]\backslash i},\mathbf{y}_{[n]\backslash i}}\prod_{j\in[n]\backslash i}\nu_{j\rightarrow i}(x_{j},y_{j})\exp\left\{\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda^{(l)}}{n}}A^{(l)}_{i,j}x_{i}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\right\}+o(1). $$

#### Parametrization.

To proceed, we need a simple parametrization for any distribution on $(x,y)\in\{\pm 1\}^{L+L_{1}}$ . Inspired by synchronization problems on unitary groups Perry et al. (2018) and Boolean analysis O’Donnell (2014), we consider the following $2^{L+L_{1}}$ different functions on $\{\pm 1\}^{L+L_{1}}$ , which are indexed by each subset $I\subset[L+L_{1}]$ ,
